Model-assisted semi-supervised estimation of the Mann--Whitney probability under right censoring22 2 This research was supported by the Natural Science Foundation of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region (No. 2025D14015) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 72571102).

Hengyao Xu Affiliation: College of Mathematics and Systems Science, Xinjiang University,    Tao Tan ††thanks: Corresponding author. Email: ttan303@163.com. Affiliation: Urumqi, Xinjiang, China
Abstract

We study semi-supervised estimation of the full-lifetime Mann–Whitney probability under right censoring using finite covariate-only samples from two populations. A model-assisted estimator is constructed by adjusting censored pair comparisons with differences between labeled and auxiliary feature means. Resource weights minimize first-order variance within the working projection class. Under joint independent censoring and regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality through a four-pool influence representation that accounts for censoring distributions estimated from the same labeled records. Consistent variance estimation from all four sample pools yields Wald confidence intervals. The efficiency analysis relates variance reduction to projected comparison signals and auxiliary sample sizes and characterizes the gap to the semiparametric bound. A fixed-horizon extension accommodates half-weighted ties and the terminal mass induced by capping follow-up. Simulations show increasing precision gains with auxiliary sample size under moderate or strong projected signals, with finite-sample losses in some settings with zero or weak projected signals. A five-year Rotterdam breast-cancer comparison illustrates precision gains and variability across label allocations when auxiliary samples are formed by controlled outcome withholding.

Keywords: auxiliary covariates; cross-fitting; influence function; Mann–Whitney probability; right censoring; semi-supervised inference.

MSC 2020: Primary 62N02; Secondary 62G05, 62G20, 62D10.

1 Introduction

1.1 Background and motivation

The Mann–Whitney probability compares two event-time distributions through the ordering of independently sampled individuals (Mann and Whitney, 1947; Thas et al., 2012). For event times T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} from the respective populations, the strict full-lifetime target is

θ=ℙ⁡(T1<T2).\theta=\mathbb{P}(T_{1}<T_{2}).

For an adverse event such as death, θ\theta is the probability that an individual from population 1 experiences the event first. Under continuous event-time distributions, values below one half indicate that population 1 tends to experience the event later. The parameter compares marginal event-time distributions without imposing proportional hazards.

Right censoring obscures some pairwise orderings, so identification depends on the follow-up support and censoring mechanism. Under independent censoring and suitable support, inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) and Kaplan–Meier integration recover comparisons from observed event records (Datta et al., 2010; Chen and Datta, 2019; Fernández and Rivera, 2020). Identification of the lifetime comparison requires censoring support over the effective event-time range. A prespecified horizon instead defines a restricted comparison of capped event times, with half weight assigned to ties (Dobler and Pauly, 2018; Zhang et al., 2022); all individuals surviving beyond that horizon occupy the same terminal category.

Semi-supervised inference can use baseline covariates from individuals whose event histories are unavailable. We study two populations, each contributing labeled records and an independent covariate-only sample from the same population. Labeled records estimate how covariates predict pairwise comparison information, and the auxiliary records improve estimation of its population average, as in fully observed two-sample comparisons (Tan et al., 2025). Inference must account for variation in the auxiliary feature means and for censoring distributions estimated from the same labeled records used in the pair comparisons.

1.2 Related work

Auxiliary covariates improve estimation by refining the population average of a covariate-predictable outcome or estimating function. This principle connects model-assisted survey estimation (Särndal et al., 1992) with semi-supervised inference for means, regression parameters and general estimating equations (Zhang et al., 2019a; Chakrabortty and Cai, 2018; Song et al., 2024). For example, Gronsbell and Cai (2018) combine a calibrated outcome model with the covariate distribution estimated from unlabeled observations, while prediction-powered inference uses a related prediction-plus-correction structure (Angelopoulos et al., 2023; Angelopoulos et al., 2026). General semiparametric theory characterizes the gain through the covariate-predictable component of a supervised influence function and the relative labeled and unlabeled sample sizes (Xu et al., 2026). The observation model determines which score must be learned and how it enters feasible inference.

For two-sample comparisons, outcome information is carried by pairs. Schisterman and Rotnitzky (2001) developed auxiliary-variable estimation for KK-sample UU-statistics with missing outcomes, and Cannings and Fan (2022) studied correlation-assisted corrections that include UU-statistic applications. Kim et al. (2025) established a general semi-supervised theory for UU-statistics, including efficiency and degeneracy. The closest two-sample design is that of Tan et al. (2025), who combine semiparametric imputation of pairwise comparison information with weights balancing labeled and unlabeled contributions. Their design has independent labeled and covariate-only samples in each population, with matching covariate distributions within each population while allowing the two populations to differ. Zhang et al. (2025) extend semi-supervised methods to two-population functionals, while Xu and Tan (2026) study group-specific functionals through conditional imputation. With right censoring, the supervised pair statistic also depends on the estimated censoring distributions.

Censored pair statistics use IPCW UU-statistics to recover comparisons obscured by censoring (Datta et al., 2010; Chen and Datta, 2019); Kaplan–Meier VV- and UU-statistic theory characterizes the contribution from estimating event-time distributions (Fernández and Rivera, 2020). General results for UU-statistics with estimated nuisance parameters describe how nuisance estimation enters their limiting distributions (Desgagné et al., 2025). Censored two-sample alternatives also include empirical likelihood (Zhou and Liang, 2005) and semiparametric estimating equations (Bai et al., 2014). Covariate augmentation for censored Mann–Whitney effects has been developed for causal comparisons (Zhang et al., 2019b) and randomized trials (Zhang et al., 2020). In the latter setting, a Kaplan–Meier plug-in influence function is projected onto covariate adjustment directions under a common covariate distribution. The present sampling design gives each population its own auxiliary pool, so the expansion includes uncertainty in two population-specific auxiliary means alongside the group-specific censoring-estimation contributions.

Recent survival work uses covariates in pseudo-observation regression for conditional Mann–Whitney effects (Dobler et al., 2026) and in semi-supervised treatment rules (Li et al., 2026). Other work addresses restricted benefits and ties in fixed-horizon comparisons (Zhang et al., 2022; Dobler and Pauly, 2018). Related observation models address covariate-dependent labeling under missing at random (Su et al., 2024) and identification under dependent censoring with proxy information (Ying, 2024). We study marginal comparisons under within-population independence of censoring from event times and covariates.

1.3 Contributions and organization

We construct a model-assisted estimator of the Mann–Whitney probability for two right-censored populations with finite, population-specific auxiliary samples. It combines an IPCW pair statistic with a rectangular cross-fitted covariate adjustment. The asymptotic linear representation includes the contribution of estimating each censoring distribution from the records used in the pair comparisons. The resulting four-pool variance estimator supports feasible Wald inference. The transfer weights balance the sampling variation of the labeled and auxiliary feature means. We characterize the optimal weights within the working projection class and decompose the gap to the canonical efficiency bound into supervised-score and feature-projection components.

For comparisons through a prespecified follow-up horizon, we establish identification and inference for a half-tie probability on a fixed recording grid. The analysis incorporates the terminal atom induced by capping event times and the priority of events at shared event/censoring times. Simulations examine how signal, auxiliary sample size and finite-sample fitting costs affect precision and interval calibration. A five-year Rotterdam comparison illustrates the procedure with covariate-only samples obtained through controlled outcome withholding.

Section 2 presents the estimator, and Section 3 develops its full-lifetime theory. Section 4 gives the fixed-horizon extension. Sections 5 and 6 report the simulations and Rotterdam analysis, followed by discussion in Section 7. Appendices A and B contain auxiliary results and proofs; Appendix C supplies additional numerical results.

2 Methodology

2.1 Data structure and assumptions

For population k=1,2k=1,2, let Ok=(Yk,Δk,𝑿k)O_{k}=(Y_{k},\Delta_{k},\bm{X}_{k}), where Yk=min⁡(Tk,Ck)Y_{k}=\min(T_{k},C_{k}) and Δk=𝟏​(Tk≤Ck)\Delta_{k}=\mathbf{1}(T_{k}\leq C_{k}).

Following the two-population sampling design of Tan et al. (2025), we write the observed data in population kk as a labeled sample ℒk\mathcal{L}_{k} and an unlabeled sample 𝒰k\mathcal{U}_{k}:

ℒk={(Yk​i,Δk​i,𝑿k​i):i=1,…,nk},𝒰k={𝑿k​jU:j=1,…,Mk},k=1,2.\mathcal{L}_{k}=\{(Y_{ki},\Delta_{ki},\bm{X}_{ki}):i=1,\ldots,n_{k}\},\qquad\mathcal{U}_{k}=\{\bm{X}^{U}_{kj}:j=1,\ldots,M_{k}\},\qquad k=1,2.

The observed data thus comprise (ℒ1,𝒰1,ℒ2,𝒰2)(\mathcal{L}_{1},\mathcal{U}_{1},\mathcal{L}_{2},\mathcal{U}_{2}). Each labeled record includes an observed follow-up time, an event indicator, and covariates. Each unlabeled record includes only covariates.

Throughout the theory, n=n1+n2n=n_{1}+n_{2} is the total labeled size. Vectors and matrices are set in bold. The working feature map is denoted by 𝒖k\bm{u}_{k}; expectation, variance and covariance are written as 𝔼\mathbb{E}, Var\operatorname{Var} and Cov\operatorname{Cov}.

The estimator starts from labeled pair comparisons and adjusts for the difference between auxiliary and labeled feature means. Because the auxiliary mean is estimated, the amount of transfer depends on both sample sizes. The following assumptions specify the full-lifetime experiment.

  1. (A1)

    The four pools are mutually independent and i.i.d. within each pool. Labeled and unlabeled covariates have the same marginal law within a population. As n→∞n\to\infty, nk/n→πk>0n_{k}/n\to\pi_{k}>0 and Mk/n→λk∈(0,∞)M_{k}/n\to\lambda_{k}\in(0,\infty).

  2. (A2)

    Ck⟂(Tk,𝑿k)C_{k}\perp(T_{k},\bm{X}_{k}); TkT_{k} is nonnegative, finite almost surely and marginally nonatomic. On the effective event-time support, the cumulative censoring hazard is absolutely continuous with bounded measurable hazard rate on [0,b0][0,b_{0}] for a fixed finite b0b_{0}, with no effective censoring hazard thereafter. Also Hk​(b0)=ℙ⁡(Yk≥b0)>0H_{k}(b_{0})=\mathbb{P}(Y_{k}\geq b_{0})>0. In a bounded event-time model, changes to censoring beyond the event support are immaterial; with unbounded event times, surviving censoring mass can be at Ck=∞C_{k}=\infty.

  3. (A3)

    The feature map 𝒖k​(𝑿k)∈ℝJk\bm{u}_{k}(\bm{X}_{k})\in\mathbb{R}^{J_{k}} has fixed dimension, 𝔼​‖𝒖k‖2+η<∞\mathbb{E}\|\bm{u}_{k}\|^{2+\eta}<\infty for some η>0\eta>0, and positive-definite covariance 𝚪k\bm{\Gamma}_{k}.

  4. (A4)

    A fixed K≥2K\geq 2 partitions labeled indices into folds Ik​aI_{ka} independently of their values. All fold and training fractions have positive limiting proportions. The denominator safeguard is εn=min(0.01,n−1/4)\varepsilon_{n}=\min(0.01,n^{-1/4}).

  5. (A5)

    The limiting variance of the estimator under consideration is positive when studentized inference is asserted.

Assumptions (A1)–(A2) describe sampling and identification; Assumptions (A3)–(A5) control feature fitting, fold stability and studentization. The censoring restriction gives a positive lower bound for Gk​(t)=ℙ⁡(Ck≥t)G_{k}(t)=\mathbb{P}(C_{k}\geq t) on the effective event support and for HkH_{k} on [0,b0][0,b_{0}], supplying the uniform expansion used below. Lifetime identification requires this support beyond the observed sample times.

Within-population equality of the labeled and auxiliary covariate laws centers the feature-mean correction at its target.

2.2 Semi-supervised estimation under censoring

For independent draws from the two populations define

q⁡(O1,O2)=Δ1​Δ2​𝟏​(Y1<Y2)G1​(Y1)​G2​(Y2).q(O_{1},O_{2})=\frac{\Delta_{1}\Delta_{2}\mathbf{1}(Y_{1}<Y_{2})}{G_{1}(Y_{1})G_{2}(Y_{2})}.

Estimate GkG_{k} by a group-specific reverse Kaplan–Meier (KM) estimator fitted to all labeled observations in population kk. The fit pools labeled observations across folds within that population and remains separate between populations. Use max⁡{G^k​(Yk​i−),εn}\max\{\widehat{G}_{k}(Y_{ki}-),\varepsilon_{n}\} in the fitted kernel q^i​j\widehat{q}_{ij}. Under Assumption (A2), finite censoring times do not tie with event times; the left-limit convention is predictable. The clipping safeguard is inactive with probability tending to one.

Let PnP_{n} denote the full labeled pair average and Pa​bP_{ab} the average over I1​a×I2​bI_{1a}\times I_{2b}. Write nk​a=|Ik​a|n_{ka}=|I_{ka}| and wa​b=n1​a​n2​b/(n1​n2)w_{ab}=n_{1a}n_{2b}/(n_{1}n_{2}). For rectangular cross-fitting, I1​a×I2​bI_{1a}\times I_{2b} is the evaluation rectangle and I1​ac×I2​bcI_{1a}^{c}\times I_{2b}^{c} is its training rectangle. On the training rectangle, regress q^\widehat{q} on (1,𝒖1⊤,𝒖2⊤)⊤(1,\bm{u}_{1}^{\top},\bm{u}_{2}^{\top})^{\top} by ordinary least squares (OLS), with slope blocks 𝜷^1,a​b,𝜷^2,a​b\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{1,ab},\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{2,ab}. If an empirical Gram matrix is singular, its Moore–Penrose inverse defines the fitted slopes; under Assumption (A3), the limiting population Gram matrix is nonsingular. With ℓ1​(a,b)=a\ell_{1}(a,b)=a and ℓ2​(a,b)=b\ell_{2}(a,b)=b, define

θ^​(s1,s2)=\displaystyle\widehat{\theta}(s_{1},s_{2})={} ∑a,bwa​b​[Pa​b​q^+∑k=12sk​𝜷^k,a​b⊤​{𝒖¯kU−𝒖¯k,ℓk​(a,b)}],\displaystyle\sum_{a,b}w_{ab}\left[P_{ab}\widehat{q}+\sum_{k=1}^{2}s_{k}\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{k,ab}^{\top}\{\bar{\bm{u}}_{k}^{U}-\bar{\bm{u}}_{k,\ell_{k}(a,b)}\}\right], (1)
ck,n=\displaystyle c_{k,n}={} MkMk+nk,θ^SS=θ^​(c1,n,c2,n).\displaystyle\frac{M_{k}}{M_{k}+n_{k}},\qquad\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{SS}}=\widehat{\theta}(c_{1,n},c_{2,n}). (2)

We denote the proposed semi-supervised estimator by θ^SS\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{SS}}, the supervised estimator θ^​(0,0)=Pn​q^\widehat{\theta}(0,0)=P_{n}\widehat{q} by θ^sup\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{sup}}, and the unshrunk semi-supervised estimator θ^​(1,1)\widehat{\theta}(1,1) by θ^un\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{un}}. The three procedures use the same labeled observations and censoring estimates. The two semi-supervised procedures also share folds and regressions, differing only in the transfer weights. Weighted uses sk=ck,ns_{k}=c_{k,n} to account for the size of the auxiliary pool, and Unshrunk uses sk=1s_{k}=1.

In each population, the adjustment compares the auxiliary feature mean with the mean in the held-out labeled fold. The fitted slope converts this difference into a correction on the scale of the pairwise comparison. When the working features capture variation in the conditional comparison signal, the auxiliary mean can improve estimation of its population average. The correction also reflects uncertainty in that mean: ck,nc_{k,n} approaches zero when the auxiliary pool is small relative to the labeled pool and approaches one as its relative size grows. Corollary 1 gives the corresponding first-order variance comparison.

Each auxiliary pool estimates the feature distribution of its own population. Under Assumption (A1), the labeled and auxiliary feature means within a population estimate the same expectation, while the covariate distributions of the two populations may differ. The two corrections therefore use population-specific information to refine estimation of the marginal ordering probability. Their relative contributions depend on both the precision of the feature means and the extent to which the fitted features explain comparison outcomes involving that population. An asymmetric design can thus provide a precise auxiliary mean for one group and a less precise mean for the other, motivating separate transfer weights and separate contributions to the four-pool variance.

The regression slopes are fitted on pairs outside both held-out folds, whereas each censoring distribution is estimated using all labeled observations in its population. The influence-function calculation below accounts for this shared censoring fit when constructing the standard error.

The intercept cancels from the difference of feature means. An additive fit avoids constructing an unlabeled pair matrix. In a complete training rectangle the two centered feature blocks have exactly zero empirical cross-covariance, so the two slope blocks can be computed from pair row and column means. Unequal folds require the displayed weights: ∑a​bwa​b​Pa​b​q^=Pn​q^\sum_{ab}w_{ab}P_{ab}\widehat{q}=P_{n}\widehat{q} exactly. Replacing every fitted slope by a fixed population slope similarly aggregates held-out means into the full labeled mean.

Algorithm 1 summarizes estimation and inference.

3 Theoretical properties

Censoring estimation changes the labeled score on which covariate transfer acts. We first identify that complete score, then quantify the variance recovered by finite auxiliary samples and its relation to the canonical benchmark.

Remark 1.

The covariance identity in Lemma 1 records how estimating censoring weights on the same labeled observations used for the pair comparisons changes the complete labeled score: Cov⁡(gk,ψk)=−Var⁡(ψk)\operatorname{Cov}(g_{k},\psi_{k})=-\operatorname{Var}(\psi_{k}) and hence Var⁡(dk)=Var⁡(gk)−Var⁡(ψk)\operatorname{Var}(d_{k})=\operatorname{Var}(g_{k})-\operatorname{Var}(\psi_{k}). Remark 2.

The four-pool sampling design follows Tan et al. (2025) and shares the residual-plus-transfer structure of semi-supervised UU-statistics (Kim et al., 2025). For right-censored comparisons, the labeled score dk=gk+ψkd_{k}=g_{k}+\psi_{k} includes the effect of estimating each censoring distribution by Kaplan–Meier using the same group-specific labeled records that enter the pair statistic. This contribution and the sampling variation in the two finite auxiliary pools both enter the variance used for inference. Censored Mann–Whitney augmentation in randomized trials (Zhang et al., 2020) uses a common covariate distribution across groups. Here each auxiliary pool represents its own population, allowing distinct covariate distributions and population-specific resource weights. Section 5.4 compares the resulting variance reductions in a common submodel.

The two parts of the expansion distinguish outcome-bearing information from uncertainty in the auxiliary feature means. Their relative sampling rates determine the optimal amount of transfer in the stated class.

3.2 Optimal transfer weights

Write 𝒄=(c1,c2)\bm{c}=(c_{1},c_{2}), VSS=V⁡(c1,c2)V_{\mathrm{SS}}=V(c_{1},c_{2}), and let Vsup=∑kπk−1​Var⁡(dk)V_{\mathrm{sup}}=\sum_{k}\pi_{k}^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(d_{k}). Expanding (5) gives

V⁡(𝒔)=Vsup−∑k{2​skπk−sk2​(1πk+1λk)}​Var⁡(pk).V(\bm{s})=V_{\mathrm{sup}}-\sum_{k}\left\{\frac{2s_{k}}{\pi_{k}}-s_{k}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{\pi_{k}}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{k}}\right)\right\}\operatorname{Var}(p_{k}). (6)
Corollary 1.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1, the variance V⁡(𝐬)V(\bm{s}) in (6) is minimized over 𝐬∈ℝ2\bm{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} at sk=cks_{k}=c_{k}, k=1,2k=1,2. The minimizer in coordinate kk is unique when Var⁡(pk)>0\operatorname{Var}(p_{k})>0; when Var⁡(pk)=0\operatorname{Var}(p_{k})=0, V⁡(𝐬)V(\bm{s}) does not depend on that coordinate. In particular,

Vsup−VSS\displaystyle V_{\mathrm{sup}}-V_{\mathrm{SS}} =∑kckπk​Var⁡(pk)≥0,\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\frac{c_{k}}{\pi_{k}}\operatorname{Var}(p_{k})\geq 0,

The unshrunk gain is instead Vsup−V⁡(1,1)=∑k(πk−1−λk−1)​Var⁡(pk)V_{\mathrm{sup}}-V(1,1)=\sum_{k}(\pi_{k}^{-1}-\lambda_{k}^{-1})\operatorname{Var}(p_{k}).

The proof is given in Appendix B.3.

Remark 3.

At finite limiting ratios, ck=λk/(πk+λk)c_{k}=\lambda_{k}/(\pi_{k}+\lambda_{k}) reflects the relative precision of the labeled and auxiliary means and equals 1/21/2 when their asymptotic sizes are equal. For finite positive limiting ratios, weighting reduces the first-order variance relative to unshrunk transfer whenever at least one group has positive projected variance. If Var⁡(pk)=0\operatorname{Var}(p_{k})=0, the first-order variance is unchanged by transfer in that coordinate; the finite-sample example in Appendix B.9 shows how estimating a zero-signal adjustment can still affect precision.

The relevant broader class fixes the supervised influence function dkd_{k}. For centered square-integrable functions hk​(𝑿k)h_{k}(\bm{X}_{k}) define

Vd​(h)=∑k{πk−1​Var⁡(dk−hk)+λk−1​Var⁡(hk)}.V_{d}(h)=\sum_{k}\{\pi_{k}^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(d_{k}-h_{k})+\lambda_{k}^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(h_{k})\}. (7)

Conditional centering and completion of squares yield

Vd∗\displaystyle V_{d}^{*} =∑k{πk−1​𝔼​Var⁡(dk∣𝑿k)+(πk+λk)−1​Var⁡(bk)},\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\left\{\pi_{k}^{-1}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Var}(d_{k}\mid\bm{X}_{k})+(\pi_{k}+\lambda_{k})^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(b_{k})\right\},
Vd​(h)−Vd∗\displaystyle V_{d}(h)-V_{d}^{*} =∑k(πk−1+λk−1)​Var⁡(hk−ck​bk).\displaystyle=\sum_{k}(\pi_{k}^{-1}+\lambda_{k}^{-1})\operatorname{Var}(h_{k}-c_{k}b_{k}).

Thus ck​bkc_{k}b_{k} is optimal within the fixed-dd transfer class, and ck​pkc_{k}p_{k} is optimal in the working linear space. The residual-and-transfer principle and its finite-resource variance reduction are instances of general semi-supervised projection theory (Xu et al., 2026); the present construction supplies the specific censored supervised score and its feasible estimation. Appendix B.10 establishes first-order equivalence to an empirically centered projection update in the two-population experiment.

3.3 Semiparametric efficiency

Write Sk​(t∣𝒙)=ℙ⁡(Tk≥t∣𝑿k=𝒙)S_{k}(t\mid\bm{x})=\mathbb{P}(T_{k}\geq t\mid\bm{X}_{k}=\bm{x}) and

aX​k​(t,𝒙)\displaystyle a_{Xk}(t,\bm{x}) =𝔼{rk(Tk)∣Tk≥t,𝑿k=𝒙},\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\{r_{k}(T_{k})\mid T_{k}\geq t,\bm{X}_{k}=\bm{x}\}, (8)
ek\displaystyle e_{k} =gk+∫0b0aX​k​(t,𝑿k)Gk​(t)​d​MkC​(t),\displaystyle=g_{k}+\int_{0}^{b_{0}}\frac{a_{Xk}(t,\bm{X}_{k})}{G_{k}(t)}dM_{k}^{C}(t),
Dk\displaystyle D_{k} =dk−ek.\displaystyle=d_{k}-e_{k}.

Conditional tails on zero-risk sets may be assigned arbitrary values, since their risk-weighted contributions vanish. The marginal tail in dkd_{k} and the conditional tail in eke_{k} are different objects. The efficiency model retains Ck⟂(Tk,𝑿k)C_{k}\perp(T_{k},\bm{X}_{k}) from Assumption (A2); its censoring-score directions depend on time alone. Covariate-dependent censoring would change this tangent space and its canonical gradient.

Theorem 2.

Suppose that Assumptions (A1)–(A4) hold. For each k=1,2k=1,2, the quantities in (8) have the following properties.

(i) eke_{k} is the supervised observed-data canonical gradient for the group-kk contribution. It satisfies 𝔼⁡(ek∣𝐗k)=bk\mathbb{E}(e_{k}\mid\bm{X}_{k})=b_{k}, while DkD_{k} is orthogonal to the observed tangent space, to eke_{k}, and to square-integrable functions of 𝐗k\bm{X}_{k}.

(ii) In the four-pool experiment, the efficient influence functions in sample-mean form are (ek−ck​bk,ck​bk)(e_{k}-c_{k}b_{k},c_{k}b_{k}) for the labeled and auxiliary pools. The efficiency bound under n\sqrt{n} scaling is

Veff=∑k{πk−1​𝔼​Var⁡(ek∣𝑿k)+(πk+λk)−1​Var⁡(bk)}.V_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sum_{k}\left\{\pi_{k}^{-1}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Var}(e_{k}\mid\bm{X}_{k})+(\pi_{k}+\lambda_{k})^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(b_{k})\right\}.

(iii) For every centered square-integrable transfer hk​(𝐗k)h_{k}(\bm{X}_{k}) in the class (7), the excess variance over the efficiency bound separates into supervised-score and transfer losses:

Vd​(h)−Veff=∑k{πk−1​Var⁡(Dk)+(πk−1+λk−1)​Var⁡(hk−ck​bk)}.V_{d}(h)-V_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sum_{k}\left\{\pi_{k}^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(D_{k})+(\pi_{k}^{-1}+\lambda_{k}^{-1})\operatorname{Var}(h_{k}-c_{k}b_{k})\right\}.

For the proposed linear transfer, the second term is the loss from approximating the conditional comparison signal in the working feature space:

VSS−Veff=∑kVar⁡(Dk)πk+∑k(πk−1+λk−1)​ck2​Var⁡(bk−pk).V_{\mathrm{SS}}-V_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sum_{k}\frac{\operatorname{Var}(D_{k})}{\pi_{k}}+\sum_{k}(\pi_{k}^{-1}+\lambda_{k}^{-1})c_{k}^{2}\operatorname{Var}(b_{k}-p_{k}).

The proposed estimator attains VeffV_{\mathrm{eff}} if and only if Dk=0D_{k}=0 and pk=bkp_{k}=b_{k} almost surely for both populations.

The proof is given in Appendix B.4, using the observed-data projection approach to censoring efficiency (Tsiatis, 2006). That section also gives the Riesz normalization corresponding to the sample-mean coordinates in the theorem.

Remark 4.

The two terms in Theorem 2 have distinct interpretations: Var⁡(Dk)/πk\operatorname{Var}(D_{k})/\pi_{k} measures the gap between the supervised score and the canonical gradient, while the second term measures approximation of bkb_{k} by the working features. Example 1 sets the latter loss to zero and isolates the supervised-score component.

Example 1.

Take independent X1,X2∼Bernoulli⁡(1/2)X_{1},X_{2}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2), with T1|X1=0∼Unif⁡[2,3]T_{1}\mid X_{1}=0\sim\operatorname{Unif}[2,3], T1|X1=1∼Unif⁡[4,5]T_{1}\mid X_{1}=1\sim\operatorname{Unif}[4,5], and T2∼Unif⁡[2,5]T_{2}\sim\operatorname{Unif}[2,5] independent of (X1,X2)(X_{1},X_{2}). The marginal comparison probability is θ=1/2\theta=1/2. The conditional comparison signals are b1​(X1)=(1−2​X1)/3b_{1}(X_{1})=(1-2X_{1})/3 and b2​(X2)=0b_{2}(X_{2})=0, so the linear working features uk=Xku_{k}=X_{k} give the exact projections pk=bkp_{k}=b_{k}. With π1=π2=1/2\pi_{1}=\pi_{2}=1/2 and λ1=λ2=5/2\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=5/2, the asymptotic variances are

Vsup=19/27,VSS=Vd∗=14/27,Veff=8/27.V_{\mathrm{sup}}=19/27,\qquad V_{\mathrm{SS}}=V_{d}^{*}=14/27,\qquad V_{\mathrm{eff}}=8/27.

The working-projection loss is zero, while VSS−Veff=2/9V_{\mathrm{SS}}-V_{\mathrm{eff}}=2/9 remains as the censoring-information component.

The full-lifetime results allow event-time atoms when effective censoring remains continuous, with strict functions r1​(t)=ℙ⁡(T2>t)r_{1}(t)=\mathbb{P}(T_{2}>t) and r2​(t)=F1​(t−)r_{2}(t)=F_{1}(t-). Event ties receive zero weight. The fixed-grid proof handles shared event–censoring atoms using the finite-product derivative in (B.5).

The four independent pools contribute separate sample variances. Within a labeled pool, however, the pair projection and censoring contribution must be combined before taking a variance. The following construction estimates that complete score.

The Gaussian multiplier in Appendix B.5 perturbs these estimated influence-function scores.

When clinical follow-up is limited to a specified horizon, the following capped comparison supplies a target supported by that observation window.

4 Fixed-horizon extension

For a fixed integer horizon τ\tau, define recorded-day event times capped at the horizon, Sk=Tk∧τS_{k}=T_{k}\wedge\tau, and

θτ=𝔼⁡{H⁡(S1,S2)},H⁡(s,t)=𝟏​(s<t)+12​𝟏​(s=t).\theta_{\tau}=\mathbb{E}\{H(S_{1},S_{2})\},\qquad H(s,t)=\mathbf{1}(s<t)+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{1}(s=t). (10)

The relation to the full strict target is

θτ−θ=\displaystyle\theta_{\tau}-\theta={} 12​ℙ​(T1=T2<τ)+12​ℙ​(T1≥τ,T2≥τ)\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}(T_{1}=T_{2}<\tau)+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}(T_{1}\geq\tau,T_{2}\geq\tau)
−ℙ⁡(T1<T2,T1≥τ,T2≥τ).\displaystyle-\mathbb{P}(T_{1}<T_{2},T_{1}\geq\tau,T_{2}\geq\tau).

This identity separates ties observed before the horizon from pairs whose ordering is lost beyond it. If event times are almost surely finite, the capped half-tie parameter tends to the full half-tie probability as τ\tau increases; the limit agrees with the strict target when original ties have probability zero.

Higher values indicate earlier events in population 1. Ties include observed same-day events and the terminal tie when both capped times equal τ\tau. Each capped distribution has a terminal atom formed by event times at or beyond τ\tau. An unobserved ordering caused by early censoring is not assigned a half score.

Let Zk=Yk∧τZ_{k}=Y_{k}\wedge\tau and

Ak=𝟏​(Δk=1,Yk<τ)+𝟏​(Yk≥τ).A_{k}=\mathbf{1}(\Delta_{k}=1,Y_{k}<\tau)+\mathbf{1}(Y_{k}\geq\tau).

When Ak=1A_{k}=1, Sk=ZkS_{k}=Z_{k} is known, including records originally censored exactly at τ\tau. Otherwise Zk=Ck<τZ_{k}=C_{k}<\tau and Sk>ZkS_{k}>Z_{k}. For this subsection, impose Assumption (H1) for each population kk:

  1. (a)

    The recorded-day grid and horizon τ\tau are fixed and finite. Both capped event times and pre-horizon censoring times take values on this prescribed grid; the four-pool sampling, feature and fold assumptions are those in Assumptions (A1), (A3) and (A4).

  2. (b)

    Censoring is jointly independent, Ck⟂(Sk,𝑿k)C_{k}\perp(S_{k},\bm{X}_{k}), on the horizon, and Gk,−​(τ)=ℙ⁡(Ck≥τ)>0G_{k,-}(\tau)=\mathbb{P}(C_{k}\geq\tau)>0.

  3. (c)

    The capped event time has positive terminal mass, ℙ⁡(Sk=τ)>0\mathbb{P}(S_{k}=\tau)>0, and each active pre-horizon censoring hazard is less than one.

  4. (d)

    The limiting variance is positive when studentized inference is asserted.

The positive terminal mass and active-risk conditions in (H1) support the finite-grid expansion. Events take priority when event and censoring times share a grid point, as specified by Δ=𝟏​(T≤C)\Delta=\mathbf{1}(T\leq C).

Under event priority, estimate the censoring hazard at t<τt<\tau by

a^k​t=d​Ck​(t)Rk​(t)−d​Ek​(t),G^k,−​(s)=∏t<s(1−a^k​t),\widehat{a}_{kt}=\frac{dC_{k}(t)}{R_{k}(t)-dE_{k}(t)},\qquad\widehat{G}_{k,-}(s)=\prod_{t<s}(1-\widehat{a}_{kt}),

where Rk​(t)=∑i𝟏​(Zk​i≥t)R_{k}(t)=\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}(Z_{ki}\geq t), d​Ek​(t)=∑i𝟏​(Zk​i=t,Ak​i=1)dE_{k}(t)=\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}(Z_{ki}=t,A_{ki}=1) and d​Ck​(t)=∑i𝟏​(Zk​i=t,Ak​i=0)dC_{k}(t)=\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}(Z_{ki}=t,A_{ki}=0). Remark 6.

Theorem 4 supplies inference for the comparison available at a prespecified follow-up horizon, as used in the Rotterdam application. The recorded-day grid, terminal tie and event-priority rule determine how boundary observations enter the score. Appendix B.7 gives completion bounds for the remaining unobserved orderings.

5 Simulation studies

We assess when finite covariate-only samples improve a censored two-sample comparison. Full-lifetime designs vary signal and resource size; fixed-horizon designs add terminal ties, alternative working features and a common submodel for comparison with trial augmentation.

The methods share labeled observations and censoring fits, and the adjusted estimators also share regressions and folds. In balanced designs, n0n_{0} and M0M_{0} denote per-population sizes; asymmetric designs list all four pool sizes. Resource levels reuse labeled samples and nested prefixes of the covariate-only pools.

Table rows denote Supervised, Unshrunk and Weighted by θ^sup\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{sup}}, θ^un\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{un}} and θ^SS\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{SS}}; fixed-horizon rows add the subscript τ\tau. Let sA2s_{A}^{2} be the Monte Carlo variance centered at method AA’s own mean. The relative variance reduction GA:B=100{1−sA2/sB2}G_{A:B}=100\{1-s_{A}^{2}/s_{B}^{2}\} compares AA with BB, with positive values favoring AA; parentheses give paired MCSE in percentage points. The asymptotic variance reduction (AVR) is the first-order working-projection prediction for Weighted relative to Supervised. The RMSE gain is RG=100​{1−RMSESS/RMSEsup}\mathrm{RG}=100\{1-\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{SS}}/\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{sup}}\}, which also reflects bias.

5.1 Full-lifetime comparisons

The full-lifetime laws vary the marginal comparison probability and the working-projection signal. Event times are generated as

T1=2+exp⁡{μ1+a​X1+1−a2​E1},T2=2+exp⁡(E2),T_{1}=2+\exp\{\mu_{1}+aX_{1}+\sqrt{1-a^{2}}E_{1}\},\qquad T_{2}=2+\exp(E_{2}),

Here Xk,Ek∼iidN⁡(0,1)X_{k},E_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}N(0,1), the working feature is uk=Xku_{k}=X_{k}, and θ=Φ(−μ1/2)\theta=\Phi(-\mu_{1}/\sqrt{2}). Censoring is independent, with G⁡(5)=0.60G(5)=0.60 except in the heavier-censoring Scenario 8, where G⁡(5)=0.35G(5)=0.35; Appendix C specifies its distribution. Scenarios 1–3 have θ=0.50\theta=0.50 and a=0,0.50,0.85a=0,0.50,0.85, corresponding to zero, moderate and strong working-projection signal. Each uses n0=200,800n_{0}=200,800 and M0/n0=1,2,5M_{0}/n_{0}=1,2,5. Scenarios 4–8 vary the comparison probability or censoring and are specified in Appendix C.

Within each repetition, the same event-history sample is used at all auxiliary sample sizes, isolating the contribution of the auxiliary pool. Table 1 summarizes 8,000 repetitions for each combination of signal, labeled size and auxiliary ratio. At n0=200n_{0}=200, increasing M0M_{0} from 200 to 1,000 raises the weighted gain from 3.04% to 5.69% under moderate signal and from 12.31% to 20.36% under strong signal. The zero-signal cells show small losses. Bias is small relative to empirical sampling variation. Figure 1 places these precision differences alongside the zero-signal error distribution.

When M0=n0M_{0}=n_{0}, unshrunk transfer has zero first-order gain, while finite-resource weighting recovers half of the transferable projection variance. As auxiliary pools grow, the weighted and unshrunk gains approach one another. At n0=800n_{0}=800 under strong signal, the weighted gain rises from 13.83% (MCSE 0.70) at ratio 1 to 22.76% (0.81) at ratio 5, close to predictions of 13.27% and 22.11%. Zero-projection cells show small negative empirical gains, consistent with slope-estimation costs when no first-order gain is available.

Four-pool sampling allows the two populations to contribute different amounts of auxiliary information. Scenario 22 places a linear signal in both groups and varies their labeled and auxiliary sizes. Scenarios 23 and 24 share a quadratic event mechanism but use linear versus linear-plus-quadratic features. Scenario 25 uses different covariate distributions across groups, retaining the same covariate distribution within each labeled/auxiliary pair. Their exact laws are given in Appendix C.

Table 2 shows gains from both auxiliary pools as well as from their allocation. In the balanced dual-signal configuration, the weighted gain rises from 8.86% to 14.27% as the ratio increases from one to five. With labeled sizes (200,400)(200,400), the two asymmetric auxiliary allocations give weighted gains of 7.57% and 9.87%; the corresponding unshrunk gains are −36.53%-36.53\% and −10.69%-10.69\%. Figure 3(a) compares these allocations with the first-order prediction. The separate resource weights accommodate the unequal precision of the two auxiliary means.

The same table distinguishes information present in the event mechanism from information represented by the working features. At n0=800n_{0}=800, the quadratic law gives a −0.57%-0.57\% gain with a linear feature and 8.66% after the quadratic feature is included. Under different population covariate laws, the weighted gains are 11.81% and 13.94% at n0=200n_{0}=200 and 800. These settings retain matching labeled and auxiliary covariate laws within each population while allowing the two populations to differ. The nonzero-effect rows at θ=0.35\theta=0.35 and 0.65 are summarized in Table C.1, which also reports method-specific calibration.

For the usual-censoring, strong-signal Scenario 3 in Table 1, Weighted coverage is 94.34% at n0=200n_{0}=200 and M0/n0=5M_{0}/n_{0}=5 (Wilson interval 93.81%–94.82%). Under heavier censoring in Scenario 8, Weighted coverage is 94.4% and 95.1% at n0=200n_{0}=200 and 800, respectively, when M0/n0=1M_{0}/n_{0}=1; at ratio 5 it is 94.58% and 94.95% (Table C.1). Figure 3(c,e) gives the matched coverage and SE-calibration comparisons.

5.2 Fixed-horizon comparisons

The fixed-horizon designs examine a different observed-data problem: event and censoring times can coincide, and capping follow-up creates a positive terminal atom. On the grid {0,…,4}\{0,\ldots,4\} we use event priority and the half-tie target of Theorem 4. The 12 law/feature settings vary projected signal, censoring, resource ratio and working features. One setting records a continuous latent event time on a grid before capping; its target is the recorded-grid probability. Scenarios 9–12 have zero, weak, moderate and strong working-projection signal, respectively. Scenarios 13–14 share a quadratic event law and use linear versus linear-plus-quadratic features. Scenarios 15–16 combine weak signal with heavy versus overlap censoring; Scenarios 17–18 use weak signal and auxiliary-to-labeled ratios 0.25 versus 5. Scenario 19 has a larger group contrast (θτ=0.599225\theta_{\tau}=0.599225); Scenario 20 uses recorded-grid exponential event times (θτ=0.593044\theta_{\tau}=0.593044). Unless stated otherwise, the ratio is one and censoring is light; Scenario 20 uses overlap censoring. Conditional PMFs are specified in Appendix C.1.1.

The fixed-horizon kernel treats two event times at or beyond the horizon as a terminal tie. Censoring before the horizon can leave the pairwise ordering unresolved. The second row of Figure 1 shows the resulting error distributions, and Table 3 compares all three methods at n0=240n_{0}=240. Moderate and strong projections give gains close to the first-order predictions of about 3% and 8%. Under weak projection, little variance is available to recover, and estimating the correction can erase that small gain.

The paired working-feature comparison in Figure C.1 separates these two sources of information. A linear feature has zero projection under the centered quadratic law, whereas a quadratic feature makes that signal available for transfer. The fits use the same observed data and folds. The larger-sample results in Table C.2 show how this feature advantage develops as the labeled sample grows.

5.3 Auxiliary sample size and finite-sample performance

The fixed-horizon resource study includes Scenario 21, which combines the strong-signal event law of Scenario 12 with overlap censoring and ratios 0.25, 1 and 5 at n0=240,960n_{0}=240,960. Sample-size paths for Scenarios 14 and 20 use n0=480,1920n_{0}=480,1920 under the same respective laws; the zero-, weak- and strong-signal comparisons use n0=240n_{0}=240. Table 4 and Figure 3 report the replication counts and results.

Table 4 quantifies the cost of an imprecise auxiliary mean when the pool is small. At n0=240n_{0}=240 and ratio 0.25, unshrunk transfer increases variance by 45.89%, whereas weighting reduces it by 3.01%. At ratio five and n0=960n_{0}=960, the weighted gain is 12.53% (MCSE 0.68); RMSE changes follow the same direction in these cells. Zero- and weak-signal configurations show small losses, where little projected variance is available to offset regression fitting variability.

The sample-size paths in Figure 3(b) follow the quadratic-feature and recorded-grid laws from n0=240n_{0}=240 to 1,920. At the larger sizes, empirical gains approach the first-order values of 2.97% and 5.23%, respectively, with pointwise intervals showing the paired Monte Carlo uncertainty. In the matched calibration panels (c)–(f), MeanSE/EmpSD remains near one and coverage varies around 95%; the cell-wise Wilson intervals show where small departures are most apparent.

Coverage can also fall below the nominal level in full-lifetime designs that satisfy the model assumptions. Table C.3 reports the settings with the lowest coverage and shows how the estimated standard errors compare with the observed dispersion.

5.4 Comparison with covariate augmentation

To compare the two adjustments, we use the same supervised score and fixed working space, a common covariate law and balanced labeled counts. At Mk=nk=n0M_{k}=n_{k}=n_{0}, trial augmentation reduces first-order variance by Var⁡(p1−p2)/(2​n0)\operatorname{Var}(p_{1}-p_{2})/(2n_{0}), while four-pool transfer reduces it by {Var⁡(p1)+Var⁡(p2)}/(2​n0)\{\operatorname{Var}(p_{1})+\operatorname{Var}(p_{2})\}/(2n_{0}). Subtracting the trial reduction from the four-pool reduction gives Cov⁡(p1,p2)/n0\operatorname{Cov}(p_{1},p_{2})/n_{0}. Appendix B.8 derives the comparison for general auxiliary sizes and relates it to trial augmentation on a fixed grid.

In the moderate- and strong-signal examples, the trial-augmentation direction cancels. In the recorded-grid example, its theoretical reduction is about 10.37%, compared with 5.23% for Weighted. The paired results show that the relative value of labeled imbalance adjustment and auxiliary-pool transfer depends on the direction as well as the amount of covariate information.

The numerical comparison retains the common covariate law and balanced labeled counts. It varies the auxiliary ratio across three levels for each of six fixed-horizon mechanisms, with 960 labeled observations per population. Trial augmentation follows the labeled-covariate adjustment structure studied for censored Mann–Whitney effects in randomized trials (Zhang et al., 2020); the weighted estimator also uses the specified covariate-only pool. Figure 4 expresses each variance relative to the same supervised variance: values below one indicate a precision gain. This common scale shows both the resource response of the weighted procedure and the precision available from labeled imbalance adjustment.

Table 5 reports the direct paired contrasts. In Scenario 12, weighted variance is lower than that of fixed-linear-basis trial augmentation by 2.49%, 7.77% and 12.78% as the auxiliary ratio increases. In Scenario 20 the corresponding gains are −10.68%-10.68\%, −6.73%-6.73\% and −3.56%-3.56\%, with trial augmentation more precise. Its nonzero imbalance direction already captures useful information from the labeled samples; expanding the auxiliary pool narrows the difference. Together with the common-score formula, these comparisons identify signal direction and resource availability as distinct determinants of the preferred adjustment. The numerical comparison uses fixed-basis learners; additional precision and calibration results for both trial-augmentation bases appear in Table C.4, where the fixed-basis procedures are labeled Trial aug. (linear) and Trial aug. (categorical).

6 Application to the Rotterdam cohort

6.1 Data and analysis design

The Rotterdam tumor-bank cohort pairs baseline prognostic information with right-censored mortality records. We use the survival 3.8-3 dataset, with death measured from surgery (dtime/death) (Royston and Altman, 2013; Therneau, 2026). The eligible cohort contains 2,982 unique patients: 1,312 premenopausal patients in population 1 and 1,670 postmenopausal patients in population 2. Their age and disease-characteristic distributions are summarized in Table 6; the target is a descriptive comparison of these populations.

The target is the five-year recorded-day half-tie probability θ1825\theta_{1825} in (10), covered by Theorem 4. Values below 0.5 favor later capped death times in population 1. Figure 5(a) shows the full-cohort mortality curves, and Table 6 reports each patient’s observation status at five years.

At a prespecified allocation, half of each population contributes (Y,Δ,𝑿)(Y,\Delta,\bm{X}) and the other half contributes baseline covariates only. The labeled sizes are 656 and 835, respectively. Primary features are age/10, log positive nodes, two tumor-size indicators and ordinal grade; the basic feature set keeps age and log nodes. We form the covariate-only samples by withholding outcome records for the remaining cohort members. The retained features are measured at or around surgery, although individual pathology-report availability dates are unavailable.

The primary labeled partition has 472 and 582 patients at risk at five years, with event-priority censoring-survival estimates of 0.9402 and 0.9483. Figure C.2 summarizes the corresponding risk sets and weights across all 1,000 allocations at each budget.

6.2 Estimates and precision

At the prespecified primary allocation, the weighted estimate is 0.4795 with SE 0.0110 and a 95% interval of [0.4578, 0.5011] (Table 7(A)). The estimate is below 0.5, while its interval includes 0.5. Weighting reduces the fitted SE relative to supervised estimation without materially separating the three point estimates at this allocation.

The allocation distribution places the primary estimate in context. The weighted estimate lies 2.57 allocation SDs above the repeated-allocation mean of 0.4597, with 994 of the 1,000 repeated estimates below it (Figure 5(c)). The descriptive full-record supervised estimate is 0.4599.

The three precision summaries in Table 7(B) correspond to different sampling procedures. At the primary allocation, the fitted influence-function variance is 7.15% lower for Weighted than for Supervised. Repeated outcome withholding varies the label allocation conditional on the observed cohort and gives a 13.83% variance gain (MCSE 2.19 percentage points). Patient-level bootstrap resampling stratified by population and followed by a new allocation varies the sampled patients as well as the allocation and gives a 4.55% gain (MCSE 1.67 percentage points).

Figure 5(b) and Table 7(C) show how this allocation precision changes with the label budget. At 25% and 75% labeled, the group-specific labeled sizes are (328,417)(328,417) and (984,1252)(984,1252), with covariate-only sizes (984,1253)(984,1253) and (328,418)(328,418). A larger labeled pool leaves a smaller auxiliary pool within this fixed cohort. Weighted gains remain positive at the three budgets; unshrunk transfer increases allocation variance by 139.14% at 75% labeled. This contrast illustrates why the precision of the remaining auxiliary mean matters alongside the number of outcome-bearing records.

In Figure 5(d), mean influence-function SE and bootstrap SD are close for all three methods; their ratio is 0.996 for Weighted. Table C.5 gives the method-specific summaries.

Feature ablation shows an expanded-minus-basic allocation-gain difference of 0.24 percentage points (MCSE 0.93) at the 50% budget. Paired intervals include zero at all three budgets (Table ), so the expanded feature set has no resolved incremental gain in this cohort.

6.3 Sensitivity to censoring assumptions

A five-year group-stratified model relates surgery year to observed follow-up and gives a censoring hazard ratio of 1.817 per surgery year (95% interval [1.652, 1.998]); the corresponding observed-death hazard ratio is 0.973 ([0.950, 0.996]). The data documentation notes that death information may be updated after recurrence follow-up has ended (Therneau, 2026). Individual administrative cutoffs and censoring reasons are unavailable, and surgery year is absent from the primary working features. This calendar-time structure poses a substantive risk to the working assumption Ck⟂(Sk,Xk)C_{k}\perp(S_{k},X_{k}).

At the primary allocation, the prespecified alternatives differ from supervised marginal IPCW (0.481482) by approximately −0.0023-0.0023 to 0.00170.0017 (Table 8). Period-stratified IPCW estimates the censoring distribution separately for surgeries through 1987 and from 1988 onward. Within each group, we combine the period-specific event distributions using the period proportions of either the labeled patients or the complete cohort. Conditional IPCW uses Cox censoring models with linear or spline terms for surgery year. Outcome-regression standardization averages the fitted outcome distributions over the baseline covariates of either the labeled patients or the complete cohort. All outcome and censoring models use labeled records; cohort standardization additionally uses baseline information from the covariate-only patients.

Across 100 prespecified allocations, outcome standardization produced larger shifts than at the primary allocation and more variable shifts than the censoring-model alternatives. The spline censoring model failed to fit in 3 allocations (Table C.6).

7 Discussion

Auxiliary covariates improve first-order precision when they explain variation in the score for ordering event times across populations. The estimator adjusts the comparisons available from censored records by using auxiliary samples to estimate the feature means in each population. The variance calculation retains the covariance induced by using the same labeled records to form pairs and estimate the censoring distributions.

The resource weights matter most when the feature means in the auxiliary pools are imprecise. In the strong-signal resource experiments, the variance gains increase with the auxiliary sample sizes and track the first-order predictions. Weighted and unshrunk adjustments become closer as auxiliary information grows, while at zero or weak projection even a modest cost of fitting the slopes can offset the available gain. A contrast between the two labeled groups can itself capture a useful signal, so the relative value of auxiliary sampling depends on both the size of the pools and the direction of the two group-specific projections.

The five-year Rotterdam comparison illustrates how these gains should be interpreted when the follow-up window is part of the scientific question. The fixed allocation describes the precision of one analysis, whereas reallocating the labels shows how that precision depends on which patients contribute outcomes. The patient bootstrap puts this allocation variation in the context of patient sampling. The spread across allocations also puts the relatively high point estimate from the primary allocation in perspective.

The association between surgery year and follow-up in Rotterdam motivates extending the method to conditional censoring, which would change both identification and the influence function used for inference. Studies that obtain auxiliary covariates from external cohorts face a second design question: how to use those measurements when their distribution differs from that of the patients with observed follow-up. In either setting, the benefit of richer working features must be weighed against the accuracy with which their effects can be estimated from the labeled records.

Consequently the logarithm of the product-limit differs from the negative Nelson–Aalen estimator by Oℙ​(m−1)O_{\mathbb{P}}(m^{-1}). Taylor expansion yields

G⁡(t)G^​(t−)−1=1m​∑iLi​(t)+Oℙ​(m−1)\frac{G(t)}{\widehat{G}(t-)}-1=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i}L_{i}(t)+O_{\mathbb{P}}(m^{-1}) (A.1)

uniformly on the effective event support. Beyond b0b_{0}, both the true and observable censoring contributions are constant; the martingale integral is stopped at b0b_{0}. If event support is bounded, censoring changes beyond it are unobservable and irrelevant. With unbounded TT, a surviving censoring mass at infinity allows positive GG throughout. Since the denominator lower bound is positive and εn→0\varepsilon_{n}\to 0, clipping is inactive with probability tending to one.

The expansion uses the positive effective risk in (A2). When censoring hazards have fixed positive jumps, the finite-product derivative in Section B.6 gives the corresponding expansion. ∎

Lemma A.2.

Suppose that Assumptions (A1)–(A4) hold. The supervised estimator satisfies

θ^sup−θ=∑k=12PL,k​{gk+ψk}+Oℙ​(n−1).\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{sup}}-\theta=\sum_{k=1}^{2}P_{L,k}\{g_{k}+\psi_{k}\}+O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1}).
Proof.

We derive the supervised expansion, accounting for observations shared between the comparison pairs and the censoring estimator. Let q∘=q−θ−g1−g2q^{\circ}=q-\theta-g_{1}-g_{2}. Its conditional mean is zero given either pair observation. In the variance of Pn​q∘P_{n}q^{\circ}, pairs sharing only one index have zero covariance after conditioning on that observation, and disjoint pairs are independent. Only pairs sharing both indices contribute. Thus

Var⁡(Pn​q∘)=𝔼​{(q∘)2}n1​n2=O⁡(n−2),Pn​q−θ=∑kPL,k​gk+Oℙ​(n−1).\operatorname{Var}(P_{n}q^{\circ})=\frac{\mathbb{E}\{(q^{\circ})^{2}\}}{n_{1}n_{2}}=O(n^{-2}),\qquad P_{n}q-\theta=\sum_{k}P_{L,k}g_{k}+O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1}).

Using (A.1), the first-order contribution from estimating G1G_{1} is

B1​n=1n12​n2​∑i,l,jq⁡(O1​i,O2​j)​L1​l​(Y1​i).B_{1n}=\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}n_{2}}\sum_{i,l,j}q(O_{1i},O_{2j})L_{1l}(Y_{1i}). (A.2)

Uniform inverse-weight products and their quadratic errors have total remainder Oℙ​(n−1)O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1}), because qq is bounded. In (A.2), l=il=i contributes only n1​n2n_{1}n_{2} bounded terms and is Oℙ​(n1−1)O_{\mathbb{P}}(n_{1}^{-1}). Its expectation need not be zero.

For i≠li\neq l there are three independent units, with two roles from the first population. Let f⁡(i,l,j)=q⁡(i,j)​Ll​(Yi)f(i,l;j)=q(i,j)L_{l}(Y_{i}). Fixing the pair role ii or jj gives zero one-unit projection, because 𝔼​Ll​(t)=0\mathbb{E}L_{l}(t)=0 at deterministic tt. Fixing the nuisance role ll and exchanging bounded integrals gives

𝔼⁡{f⁡(i,l,j)∣O1​l}=∫0b0A1​(s)H1​(s)​d​M1​lC​(s)=ψ1​(O1​l).\mathbb{E}\{f(i,l;j)\mid O_{1l}\}=\int_{0}^{b_{0}}\frac{A_{1}(s)}{H_{1}(s)}dM^{C}_{1l}(s)=\psi_{1}(O_{1l}).

After subtracting ψl\psi_{l}, the residual is degenerate in every one-unit role. Two residual triples with at most one shared unit have zero covariance, including cross-role matches of the first-population units. Nonzero covariances require at least two shared units. Their number is O⁡(n4)O(n^{4}) against a squared normalizer of order n6n^{6}; bounded summands give residual variance O⁡(n−2)O(n^{-2}). This count expressly includes index interchange between the pair and nuisance roles. Therefore

B1​n=n1−1n1​PL,1​ψ1+Oℙ​(n−1)=PL,1​ψ1+Oℙ​(n−1).B_{1n}=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{1}}P_{L,1}\psi_{1}+O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1})=P_{L,1}\psi_{1}+O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1}).

The second population is identical with its own roles. Combining both contributions with the ordinary projection proves

θ^sup−θ=∑kPL,k​(gk+ψk)+Oℙ​(n−1).\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{sup}}-\theta=\sum_{k}P_{L,k}(g_{k}+\psi_{k})+O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1}). (A.3)

The nuisance triples account for dependence between the group-specific censoring fits using all labeled folds and the pair evaluations. The Op​(n−1)O_{p}(n^{-1}) remainder follows from the compact effective-censoring assumptions in (A2), in line with same-sample expansions for censored UU-statistics (Datta et al., 2010; Chen and Datta, 2019; Fernández and Rivera, 2020). ∎

Appendix B Proofs of the main results

The proofs follow the order of the full-lifetime results, then establish the fixed-horizon extension. Technical expansions used repeatedly are stated separately in Appendix A.

The full target is θ=ℙ⁡(T1<T2)\theta=\mathbb{P}(T_{1}<T_{2}) and the kernel is q=Δ1​Δ2​𝟏​(Y1<Y2)/{G1​(Y1)​G2​(Y2)}q=\Delta_{1}\Delta_{2}\mathbf{1}(Y_{1}<Y_{2})/\{G_{1}(Y_{1})G_{2}(Y_{2})\}. Given (Tk,𝑿k)(T_{k},\bm{X}_{k}),

Let 𝒗k=𝒖k−𝝁k\bm{v}_{k}=\bm{u}_{k}-\bm{\mu}_{k} and bk​(𝑿k)=𝔼⁡{rk​(Tk)∣𝑿k}−θb_{k}(\bm{X}_{k})=\mathbb{E}\{r_{k}(T_{k})\mid\bm{X}_{k}\}-\theta. Hence the intercept is θ\theta and 𝜷k=𝚪k−1​𝔼​(𝒗k​bk)\bm{\beta}_{k}=\bm{\Gamma}_{k}^{-1}\mathbb{E}(\bm{v}_{k}b_{k}). Therefore pk=𝜷k⊤​𝒗kp_{k}=\bm{\beta}_{k}^{\top}\bm{v}_{k} is the orthogonal projection of bkb_{k} and

𝔼​pk=0,𝔼⁡{(bk−pk)​𝒗k}=0,Cov⁡(gk,pk)=𝔼⁡(bk​pk)=Var⁡(pk).\mathbb{E}p_{k}=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}\{(b_{k}-p_{k})\bm{v}_{k}\}=0,\qquad\operatorname{Cov}(g_{k},p_{k})=\mathbb{E}(b_{k}p_{k})=\operatorname{Var}(p_{k}).

Finite second moments suffice for these projection identities. In the regression expansion below, slope consistency suffices because the slope error multiplies a centered feature-mean difference of order Op(n−1/2)O_{p}(n^{-1/2}).

This gives 𝔼⁡(ψ∣T,𝑿)=0\mathbb{E}(\psi\mid T,\bm{X})=0, 𝔼⁡(d∣𝑿)=b\mathbb{E}(d\mid\bm{X})=b, and Cov⁡(ψ,p)=0\operatorname{Cov}(\psi,p)=0. Independent censoring cancels its inclusion probability; Fubini gives the displayed conditional tail. The centering constant has zero covariance with a martingale integral.

Taking a=a0​(t)=𝔼⁡{r⁡(T)∣T≥t}a=a_{0}(t)=\mathbb{E}\{r(T)\mid T\geq t\} and using 𝔼⁡(SX​aX)=S​a0\mathbb{E}(S_{X}a_{X})=Sa_{0} gives Cov⁡(g,ψ)=−Var⁡(ψ)\operatorname{Cov}(g,\psi)=-\operatorname{Var}(\psi). Proof of Theorem 1.

We now combine the supervised expansion with the fitted covariate adjustment. Fix a fold pair (a,b)(a,b); its complementary indices are selected independently of values and retain positive asymptotic fractions. Two-sample LLNs apply to each integrable Gram or response kernel. They follow for bounded kernels from the index-sharing variance argument, and for general integrable kernels by truncation in L1L_{1}. The training empirical Gram converges to the positive-definite population Gram. For the fitted response,

‖P−a,−b​{𝒛⁡(q^−q)}‖≤supi,j|q^i​j−qi​j|​P−a,−b​‖𝒛‖=oℙ​(1),\|P_{-a,-b}\{\bm{z}(\widehat{q}-q)\}\|\leq\sup_{i,j}|\widehat{q}_{ij}-q_{ij}|P_{-a,-b}\|\bm{z}\|=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1),

where 𝒛=(1,𝒖1⊤,𝒖2⊤)⊤\bm{z}=(1,\bm{u}_{1}^{\top},\bm{u}_{2}^{\top})^{\top}. Hence 𝜷^a​b→pβ\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{ab}\to_{p}\beta. A fixed finite number of rectangles implies simultaneous slope consistency. Positive limiting Gram eigenvalues also make the finite-sample generalized inverse agree with the ordinary inverse with probability tending to one.

For each fold, finite feature second moments and the i.i.d. pool CLTs give 𝒖¯kU−𝒖¯k,ℓk​(a,b)=Oℙ(n−1/2)\bar{\bm{u}}^{U}_{k}-\bar{\bm{u}}_{k,\ell_{k}(a,b)}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1/2}). Thus

∑a​bwa​b(𝜷^k,a​b−𝜷k)⊤(𝒖¯kU−𝒖¯k,ℓk​(a,b))=oℙ(n−1/2).\sum_{ab}w_{ab}(\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{k,ab}-\bm{\beta}_{k})^{\top}(\bar{\bm{u}}^{U}_{k}-\bar{\bm{u}}_{k,\ell_{k}(a,b)})=o_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1/2}).

The product is op(n−1/2)o_{p}(n^{-1/2}) from the op​(1)o_{p}(1) slope error and the Op(n−1/2)O_{p}(n^{-1/2}) feature-mean difference.

The exact identities ∑bwa​b=n1​a/n1\sum_{b}w_{ab}=n_{1a}/n_{1} and ∑awa​b=n2​b/n2\sum_{a}w_{ab}=n_{2b}/n_{2} show that population-slope corrections aggregate to ∑ksk,n​𝜷k⊤​(𝒖¯kU−𝒖¯kL)\sum_{k}s_{k,n}\bm{\beta}_{k}^{\top}(\bar{\bm{u}}^{U}_{k}-\bar{\bm{u}}^{L}_{k}). Also ∑a​bwa​b​Pa​b​q^=Pn​q^\sum_{ab}w_{ab}P_{ab}\widehat{q}=P_{n}\widehat{q} exactly for unequal folds. If bounded sk,n→sks_{k,n}\to s_{k}, their differences from their limits multiply centered Oℙ(n−1/2)O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1/2}) means, giving another oℙ(n−1/2)o_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1/2}) remainder. Combine this with (A.3) to obtain the main asymptotic linear representation. The four pools are independent and their limiting influence functions have finite second moments, so the ordinary multivariate CLT gives the variance V⁡(𝒔)V(\bm{s}) in the main text. Actual ck,n=Mk/(Mk+nk)c_{k,n}=M_{k}/(M_{k}+n_{k}) meets the required convergence.

Thus consistency of the finite-dimensional regression suffices; the conditional comparison signal need not be correctly specified by the working linear model. ∎

B.3 Proof of Corollary 1

Proof of Corollary 1.

Expand the variance with h=s​ph=sp to obtain

V⁡(𝒔)=Vsup−∑k2​sk​πk−1​Var⁡(pk)+∑ksk2​(πk−1+λk−1)​Var⁡(pk).V(\bm{s})=V_{\mathrm{sup}}-\sum_{k}2s_{k}\pi_{k}^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(p_{k})+\sum_{k}s_{k}^{2}(\pi_{k}^{-1}+\lambda_{k}^{-1})\operatorname{Var}(p_{k}).

Each nonzero-signal coordinate is strictly convex and is minimized at ck=λk/(πk+λk)c_{k}=\lambda_{k}/(\pi_{k}+\lambda_{k}). Completing squares proves the gain and comparison with the unshrunk choice. Zero-signal coordinates are flat. The labeled-score covariance is Cov⁡(g,c​p)=c​Var⁡(p)\operatorname{Cov}(g,cp)=c\operatorname{Var}(p), whereas the transferred-score variance is Var⁡(c​p)=c2​Var⁡(p)\operatorname{Var}(cp)=c^{2}\operatorname{Var}(p).

For unrestricted centered L2L_{2} transfers, put ϵ=d−b\epsilon=d-b, so 𝔼⁡(ϵ∣𝑿)=0\mathbb{E}(\epsilon\mid\bm{X})=0. Then Var⁡(d−h)=𝔼​Var⁡(d∣𝑿)+Var⁡(b−h)\operatorname{Var}(d-h)=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Var}(d\mid\bm{X})+\operatorname{Var}(b-h). The identity

π−1​Var⁡(b−h)+λ−1​Var⁡(h)=(π+λ)−1​Var⁡(b)+(π−1+λ−1)​Var⁡(h−c​b)\pi^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(b-h)+\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(h)=(\pi+\lambda)^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(b)+(\pi^{-1}+\lambda^{-1})\operatorname{Var}(h-cb) (B.3)

proves the fixed-dd optimum c​bcb. Orthogonal decomposition b=p+(b−p)b=p+(b-p) then gives the optimal working-space transfer c​pcp and excess variance (π−1+λ−1)​c2​Var⁡(b−p)(\pi^{-1}+\lambda^{-1})c^{2}\operatorname{Var}(b-p). Full-model efficiency follows from the separate tangent-space argument in the proof of Theorem 2; the projection calculation gives the transfer optimum. Related auxiliary and semi-supervised projection results include Schisterman and Rotnitzky (2001); Song et al. (2024); Xu et al. (2026). ∎

B.4 Proof of Theorem 2

Proof of Theorem 2.

We establish canonical membership before deriving the product-experiment bound and evaluating Example 1. The latent model factors as PX​PT|𝑿​PCP_{X}P_{T\mid\bm{X}}P_{C}. Bounded scores can be written u⁡(𝑿)u(\bm{X}), v⁡(T,𝑿)v(T,\bm{X}) and w⁡(C)w(C) with 𝔼​u=0\mathbb{E}u=0, 𝔼⁡(v∣𝑿)=0\mathbb{E}(v\mid\bm{X})=0 and 𝔼​w=0\mathbb{E}w=0. Their observed scores are uu, B​v=𝔼⁡(v∣O)Bv=\mathbb{E}(v\mid O) and Q​w=𝔼⁡(w∣O)Qw=\mathbb{E}(w\mid O). Effective censoring-score directions have the closure generated by deterministic-time integrals ∫ℓ⁡(t)​d​MC​(t)\int\ell(t)dM^{C}(t). Censoring changes beyond the effective event support are invisible in the observed law.

The groupwise derivative of the target is 𝔼⁡[{r⁡(T)−θ}​{u⁡(𝑿)+v⁡(T,𝑿)}]\mathbb{E}[\{r(T)-\theta\}\{u(\bm{X})+v(T,\bm{X})\}], and its derivative in a censoring direction is zero. Define e=g+LaXe=g+L_{a_{X}}. Equation (B.1) implies 𝔼⁡(e∣T,𝑿)=r⁡(T)−θ\mathbb{E}(e\mid T,\bm{X})=r(T)-\theta. Hence ee represents the 𝑿\bm{X} and conditional-event derivatives, because ee is observed and 𝔼⁡(e​B​v)=𝔼⁡(e​v)\mathbb{E}(eBv)=\mathbb{E}(ev). Equation (B.2) proves ee orthogonal to every censoring score. To conclude that ee is canonical, membership in the observed tangent closure must also be established.

Put m⁡(𝒙)=𝔼⁡{r⁡(T)∣𝑿=𝒙}m(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\{r(T)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\} and

J⁡(t,𝒙)=∫0t∧b0aX​(s,𝒙)G⁡(s)​d​ΛC​(s),v∗​(t,𝒙)=r⁡(t)G⁡(t)−J⁡(t,𝒙)−m⁡(𝒙).J(t,\bm{x})=\int_{0}^{t\wedge b_{0}}\frac{a_{X}(s,\bm{x})}{G(s)}d\Lambda^{C}(s),\qquad v_{*}(t,\bm{x})=\frac{r(t)}{G(t)}-J(t,\bm{x})-m(\bm{x}).

These functions are bounded under the support and hazard assumptions even when TT is unbounded. 𝔼{r(T)/G(T)∣T>y,𝒙}\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\{r(T)/G(T)\mid T>y,\bm{x}\} =aX​(y,𝒙)G⁡(y)+1SX​(y)​∫yb0SX​(s)​aX​(s,𝒙)G⁡(s)​d​ΛC​(s),\displaystyle=\frac{a_{X}(y,\bm{x})}{G(y)}+\frac{1}{S_{X}(y)}\int_{y}^{b_{0}}\frac{S_{X}(s)a_{X}(s,\bm{x})}{G(s)}d\Lambda^{C}(s),
𝔼{J(T,𝒙)∣T>y,𝒙}\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\{J(T,\bm{x})\mid T>y,\bm{x}\} =J⁡(y,𝒙)+1SX​(y)​∫yb0SX​(s)​aX​(s,𝒙)G⁡(s)​d​ΛC​(s)\displaystyle=J(y,\bm{x})+\frac{1}{S_{X}(y)}\int_{y}^{b_{0}}\frac{S_{X}(s)a_{X}(s,\bm{x})}{G(s)}d\Lambda^{C}(s)

hold for censoring-almost-every yy. The future integrals cancel. It follows that

e=b⁡(𝑿)+B​v∗​(O).e=b(\bm{X})+Bv_{*}(O). (B.4)

The two terms are bounded legitimate 𝑿\bm{X} and conditional-event score directions. Bounded exponential tilts construct dominated submodels, preserve censoring independence and finite moments, and locally preserve positivity and the fixed effective support. Thus ee is a tangent member as well as a derivative representer and is the canonical gradient. This membership argument identifies the canonical gradient for the full observed-data model, beyond the minimum within the transfer class. The conditional risk-tail structure is in line with standard censoring efficiency theory (Tsiatis, 2006; Zhang et al., 2019b).

To identify the component outside this tangent space, let D=d−e=La0−aXD=d-e=L_{a_{0}-a_{X}}. Its conditional expectation given (T,𝑿)(T,\bm{X}) is zero, so it is orthogonal to 𝑿\bm{X} and conditional-event observed scores. Orthogonality to censor scores follows from 𝔼⁡{SX​(t)​(a0−aX)}=0\mathbb{E}\{S_{X}(t)(a_{0}-a_{X})\}=0. Therefore DD is in the orthogonal complement of the observed tangent space; in particular D⟂eD\perp e and D⟂f⁡(𝑿)D\perp f(\bm{X}) for any square-integrable ff. Its variance is

Var⁡(D)=∫0b0𝔼⁡[SX​(t)​{a0​(t)−aX​(t,𝑿)}2]G⁡(t)​d​ΛC​(t).\operatorname{Var}(D)=\int_{0}^{b_{0}}\frac{\mathbb{E}[S_{X}(t)\{a_{0}(t)-a_{X}(t,\bm{X})\}^{2}]}{G(t)}d\Lambda^{C}(t).

It can be positive even when the comparison signal is exactly linear.

We now incorporate the covariate-only pools. At base sample size nn, the product score inner product is ∑k{πk​𝔼​(SkL​TkL)+λk​𝔼​(SkU​TkU)}\sum_{k}\{\pi_{k}\mathbb{E}(S^{L}_{k}T^{L}_{k})+\lambda_{k}\mathbb{E}(S^{U}_{k}T^{U}_{k})\}. An ALR coordinate pair (ϕL,ϕU)(\phi^{L},\phi^{U}) corresponds to Riesz coordinates (ϕL/π,ϕU/λ)(\phi^{L}/\pi,\phi^{U}/\lambda). The 𝑿\bm{X} score is shared by the labeled and unlabeled pools; the conditional-outcome and censor scores occur only in the labeled pool. From (B.4), the efficient Riesz components are b/(π+λ)b/(\pi+\lambda) in both pools for the covariate direction and B​v∗/πBv_{*}/\pi in the labeled pool for the conditional-outcome direction. The labeled conditional component has conditional mean zero given 𝑿\bm{X}, so it is orthogonal to the shared covariate direction. For any centered covariate score uu, the two weighted inner products sum to 𝔼⁡(b​u)\mathbb{E}(bu); the labeled conditional component represents the remaining derivative through B​v∗Bv_{*}. B.5 Proof of Theorem 3

Proof of Theorem 3.

We establish variance consistency by empirical convergence of the complete scores. For known GG, a pair row mean Q1​i=n2−1​∑jq⁡(O1​i,O2​j)Q_{1i}=n_{2}^{-1}\sum_{j}q(O_{1i},O_{2j}) has conditional expectation g1​(O1​i)+θg_{1}(O_{1i})+\theta and conditional mean-squared error at most C/n2C/n_{2}, because the other-population observations are independent after conditioning on O1​iO_{1i}. Conditioning row by row and averaging the conditional error bound gives empirical L2L_{2} consistency of g^\widehat{g}; uniform q^−q=oℙ​(1)\widehat{q}-q=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1) and consistency of θ^sup\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{sup}} transfer this result to the fitted kernel.

For the bounded known kernel, finite brackets for the weighted threshold measure give a uniform LLN; fitted-weight replacement is uniformly negligible. Also H^→H\widehat{H}\to H uniformly and infH>0\inf H>0, so η^=A^/H^→η=A/H\widehat{\eta}=\widehat{A}/\widehat{H}\to\eta=A/H uniformly. Both AA and HH have bounded variation, hence η\eta has bounded variation. Similarly Λ^C→ΛC\widehat{\Lambda}^{C}\to\Lambda^{C} uniformly and its total mass is Oℙ​(1)O_{\mathbb{P}}(1).

Write ψ^i=(1−Δi)​η^​(Yi)​𝟏​(Yi≤b0)−∫0Yi∧b0η^​d​Λ^C\widehat{\psi}_{i}=(1-\Delta_{i})\widehat{\eta}(Y_{i})\mathbf{1}(Y_{i}\leq b_{0})-\int_{0}^{Y_{i}\wedge b_{0}}\widehat{\eta}\,d\widehat{\Lambda}^{C}, with compatible predictable conventions. The jump error is bounded by sup|η^−η|\sup|\widehat{\eta}-\eta|. The compensator error is controlled by this supremum times the fitted hazard mass and by the bounded-variation Stieltjes bound

supt|∫0tη​d​(Λ^C−ΛC)|≤C⁡{‖η‖∞+TV⁡(η)}​‖Λ^C−ΛC‖∞=oℙ​(1).\sup_{t}\left|\int_{0}^{t}\eta\,d(\widehat{\Lambda}^{C}-\Lambda^{C})\right|\leq C\{\|\eta\|_{\infty}+\operatorname{TV}(\eta)\}\|\widehat{\Lambda}^{C}-\Lambda^{C}\|_{\infty}=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).

Weighted slope consistency and feature moments imply, for either labeled or unlabeled empirical measure,

Ppool​|h^−c​p|2≤C​‖cn​𝜷¯−c​β‖2​Ppool​‖𝒖‖2+C​‖cn​𝜷¯‖2​‖𝒖¯U−𝝁‖2=oℙ​(1).P_{\mathrm{pool}}|\widehat{h}-cp|^{2}\leq C\|c_{n}\bar{\bm{\beta}}-c\beta\|^{2}P_{\mathrm{pool}}\|\bm{u}\|^{2}+C\|c_{n}\bar{\bm{\beta}}\|^{2}\|\bar{\bm{u}}^{U}-\bm{\mu}\|^{2}=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).

Combining the three estimates proves empirical L2L_{2} convergence of complete scores to d−c​pd-cp and c​pcp. The LLN for square-integrable true scores and Cauchy–Schwarz control of score differences give convergence of the four separately centered sample variances. Bessel denominators have the same limit, so n​SE^2→VSSn\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}^{2}\to V_{\mathrm{SS}}. The four-pool CLT and Slutsky prove Wald validity. ∎

The continuous-censoring nuisance score is a Nelson–Aalen plug-in. At an empirical censoring jump with hazard aja_{j}, the exact product-limit derivative includes the factor (1−aj)−1(1-a_{j})^{-1}. Under the risk lower bound, maxj⁡aj=Op​(n−1)\max_{j}a_{j}=O_{p}(n^{-1}) and the total fitted hazard is Op​(1)O_{p}(1), so the two score vectors differ uniformly by Op​(n−1)O_{p}(n^{-1}). The empirical L2L_{2} convergence and variance consistency therefore hold for the reported score estimator.

For a pool of size mm, let ξi\xi_{i} be independent N⁡(0,1)N(0,1) multipliers. Its perturbation is ∑iξi​(ϕ^i−ϕ^¯)/m⁡(m−1)\sum_{i}\xi_{i}(\widehat{\phi}_{i}-\bar{\widehat{\phi}})/\sqrt{m(m-1)}, whose conditional variance is sm2​(ϕ^)/ms_{m}^{2}(\widehat{\phi})/m. Four independent perturbations sum to exactly N⁡(0,SE^2)N(0,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}^{2}). This influence-function multiplier represents the Gaussian limit of the four estimated pool scores.
